title: From Foucault to the Front of the Classroom
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes opens with a pre-service teacher who can explain Foucault and Bourdieu but freezes when a class talks through an instruction, to show that knowing about teaching is not yet knowing how to teach. She argues the route from research to classroom action is uneven, citing an AERO snapshot linking confidence in judging research to using it, and says access is only part of the problem. Her proposal is practice-based teacher education using Pam Grossman's approach of representing, decomposing and approximating a practice, built into professional experience placements as a structured module on behaviour and routines. Mentors would model and rehearse a transition routine with the trainee, observe agreed behaviours and review results. She says supervising teachers must be trained as teacher educators, and that universities and schools need a shared language for practice.
points: Hughes argues that knowing about teaching has not yet become knowing how to teach for many pre-service teachers.
She notes that confidence in judging research quality makes teachers about twice as likely to consult it.
She proposes practice-based teacher education: represent a practice, decompose it into moves, then rehearse it in a supported setting.
A structured placement module on behaviour and routines would cycle through study, rehearsal, practice with pupils and review.
She says mentors need explicit training as teacher educators, and universities and schools need a shared language of practice.
quotes: It was that knowing about teaching had not yet become knowing how to teach.
Access to research is only part of the challenge. Teachers also need opportunities to make sense of it, practise what it might look like, and judge whether it is working in their context.
PSTs first encounter a practice through a representation, such as a demonstration, video or worked example. They then decompose it: breaking it into component moves, sequences and decisions.

Mentoring requires more than expertise in classroom teaching. It involves modelling practice, breaking it into learnable parts, noticing what a PST does, offering useful feedback and coaching their reasoning.
This kind of mentor training is woefully absent in Australia.
Both need to treat practice as something to analyse and develop, not merely something to perform.
If we want research to influence teaching, we need to build the conditions that help teachers use it.
